slot.brief: A charged particle enters a magnetic field at some angle; identify the direction of magnetic force and whether the speed changes, using right-hand rule.

stem: A proton enters a uniform magnetic field directed vertically downwards with a horizontal velocity directed towards the east. The magnetic force acting on the proton is directed towards the:
options: north, and its speed remains constant
south, and its speed remains constant

verdicts.working: Take east = x̂, north = ŷ, up = ẑ. F = qv×B = q(v x̂)×(−B ẑ) = qvB ŷ → north (verified numerically). Magnetic force is perpendicular to velocity, does no work, so speed stays constant.

working:
Let the horizontal east direction be along $+\hat{i}$, north along $+\hat{j}$, and vertically upward along $+\hat{k}$.

The velocity of the proton is:
$$\vec{v} = v\,\hat{i}$$

The magnetic field is directed vertically downwards:
$$\vec{B} = -B\,\hat{k}$$

The magnetic Lorentz force on a charge $q = +e$ is:
$$\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}) = e\left(v\,\hat{i} \times (-B\,\hat{k})\right) = -e v B (-\hat{j}) = e v B\,\hat{j}$$

$+\hat{j}$ corresponds to the north direction.

Since the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity ($\vec{F} \perp \vec{v}$), the power delivered by the magnetic force is:
$$P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v} = 0$$

Because the work done is zero, the kinetic energy does not change, meaning the speed of the proton remains constant.

Independent check: Take east = x̂, north = ŷ, up = ẑ. F = qv×B = q(v x̂)×(−B ẑ) = qvB ŷ → north (verified numerically). Magnetic force is perpendicular to velocity, does no work, so speed stays constant.

draft.distractor_notes:
Option B arises from confusing magnetic force with electric force, incorrectly assuming that a force in the direction of motion or sideways does work to increase speed.
Option C arises from evaluating the cross product in reverse ($\vec{B} \times \vec{v}$) or mistakenly treating the proton as having a negative charge.
Option D combines the direction reversal error with the mistaken assumption that the force opposes motion and reduces speed.
